Ticket to Ride: Why Can a Complete Hand Still Leave You Without a Route?

A single space can be cheap to claim yet determine whether you spend several more turns taking a detour. A seven-point ticket also involves more than adding seven points: completing its last connection before the deadline removes a seven-point penalty at the same time.

Alan R. Moon designed Ticket to Ride. This article uses the original USA base game and the publisher’s 2015 English reprint rules: 30 Destination Tickets, with three dealt initially and at least two retained. The official site now provides both old and new rules; the 2025 V2 changes components and the initial ticket deal. We do not combine that revision, Europe, USA 1910, or anniversary rules with this case. 2015 rules, p. 2; official rule downloads.

The three independent two-player situations below are our constructions, not playtest reports or solutions supplied by the designer. The map is public. Hands and tickets follow the game’s information rules; showing an opponent’s cards or a hidden deck order for calculation does not give that information to players. We examine three distinct constraints: whether space remains, when resources arrive, and how many actions remain after they arrive.
Angle one: The same map has different capacity at different player counts

Dallas and Houston have two parallel one-space gray routes. In a two- or three-player game, claiming one closes the other. With four or five players, different players may claim the two routes; one player can never claim both. Rules, p. 3, Claiming Routes.

Suppose the game has just begun, with Lin playing first and Jo next. Both have 45 trains, no routes, and zero route points. Lin’s four starting cards are two red and two blue; Jo has two green, one yellow, and one white. We compare two ways Lin could pursue a connection between Dallas and Houston. We are not inventing a Destination Ticket bearing those cities.

Lin can immediately spend one red to claim a gray route: one train, one point, three cards left, and this connection made. If Lin draws cards instead and Jo then spends one yellow on either parallel route, Lin cannot use the other one next turn, even with a larger hand.
The direct option has closed; the cities have not disappeared. If the following routes remain available, Lin can collect the required cards and build this particular detour:
Route · Trains and cards needed · Points from this claim
Dallas → Little Rock · 2; a set of any one color · 2
Little Rock → New Orleans · 3; a green set · 4
New Orleans → Houston · 2; a set of any one color · 2

The detour uses seven trains and at least three of Lin’s claim turns, scoring eight points. The direct route uses one train and one claim turn for one point. Two blue, three green, and two red could pay for the three listed routes, but Lin’s starting four cards are insufficient; collecting the missing cards requires additional turns. We have not established that this is the shortest or best detour in every position, or assumed Jo will always leave its routes open. Publisher’s map, pp. 2–3; scoring table, p. 4.

Two accounts matter. Those six extra spaces do produce seven more route points, but they also consume six more trains and at least two more claim actions, potentially changing how later tickets connect. Extra points do not establish that the detour has no cost. Extra distance does not establish that it is worse for every plan.

For a map designer, the number of lines printed and the number of players allowed to use them are separate decisions. In your own route prototype, hold cities, lengths, and objectives fixed while changing when parallel routes open. Record whether players contest the same connection, claim it earlier, or switch to another path. This is our proposed experiment, not a claim about Moon’s historical testing method.
Angle two: A wildcard’s price includes how and when you acquire it

Consider the six-space black route from Los Angeles to El Paso. In a separate two-player game, each player has taken one draw turn and the map is still empty. Lin has five black and one green card; Jo has six black. A legal prefix is four black cards dealt to each player, followed by Lin blindly drawing black and green, then Jo blindly drawing black and black. This stays within the twelve-card supply of each regular color.

Lin now acts. The five face-up cards are a locomotive, red, blue, yellow, and white. To compare branches, fix the hidden top two cards as locomotive, then black. Lin does not know that order, so it cannot be treated as the basis of a recommendation.
Lin’s draw sequence · Cards actually gained · Hand afterward
Take the face-up locomotive first · Only that card; no second draw · Five black, one green, one locomotive: 7 cards
Take face-up red; a locomotive replaces it; draw the second card blindly · The second card is black; neither face-up locomotive may be taken · Six black, one green, one red: 8 cards
Blindly draw a locomotive first; then take face-up red · Black replaces red afterward · Five black, one green, one locomotive, one red: 8 cards

All three hands can form a six-card black payment; the first and third use a locomotive for one black. The acquisition process differs: taking a visible locomotive consumes the whole draw action; blindly drawing one counts as just one card. The newly revealed locomotive in branch two is also unavailable as the second card. Rules, p. 3, Train Car Cards.

Branch three gaining more cards does not mean blind drawing always earns an extra card. Its result depends on the fixed hidden order. A white card on top would change the outcome of the same decision. Branch one guarantees a locomotive before the choice is made. When designing resource acquisition, track certainty, flexibility, and quantity separately rather than assigning every card a fixed price.

Time is a fourth consideration. Lin chose to draw and cannot also claim a route in that turn. Fix Jo’s next action as spending six black on Los Angeles–El Paso: Jo has 39 trains left and immediately scores 15 points. In every branch, Lin’s next turn arrives too late to claim that occupied route. The collected cards remain available for other uses, but they have not reserved space on the map.

A designer can check whether acquiring resources and committing an action occur together. Separating them makes the intervening opponent turn consequential. Public hands would make the threat easier to assess, but would not automatically remove that interval. Information rules and action timing therefore need separate consideration.
Angle three: A final turn turns a seven-point ticket into a fourteen-point swing

The third independent game is nearing its end. Lin has claimed only the two-space green Chicago–Saint Louis route and the three-space green Little Rock–New Orleans route. That is five trains used, six route points, and 40 trains remaining. Lin holds the real Chicago–New Orleans ticket worth seven points. The two separate pieces of network lack the still-open two-space gray Saint Louis–Little Rock route.

Jo’s low train supply also has a concrete history. Jo has connected the entire western path below; numbers show trains used between consecutive cities. Only the specified lane of any parallel pair is used.
Jo’s continuous path · Consecutive route lengths
Vancouver → Calgary → Winnipeg → Helena → Seattle → Portland → Salt Lake City · 3, 6, 4, 6, 1, 6
Salt Lake City → San Francisco (orange) → Los Angeles (yellow) → Phoenix → El Paso → Santa Fe → Denver · 5, 3, 3, 3, 2, 2

That totals 44 trains. Jo has just claimed the two-space gray Santa Fe–Denver route, reducing the stock from three to one and triggering the ending at the end of Jo’s turn. Lin now gets a final turn, then Jo gets a final turn, then scoring begins. The triggering player is included. The game neither ends immediately nor grants everyone else two more turns. Map, pp. 2–3; Game End, p. 4.

Lin has two blue cards to pay for the gap. A complete reachable prefix also leaves seven green, twelve purple, eleven locomotives, six white, seven orange, eight red, and one yellow: 54 cards altogether. This edition has no hand limit. The large hand establishes that missing cards are not the problem; it is not advice to hoard. These routes and hands can be reached from normal dealing through 32 Jo turns and 31 Lin turns in alternation, respecting twelve cards of each regular color and fourteen locomotives.
Compare just two specified choices, fixing Jo’s last turn as taking one visible locomotive and claiming no further route:
Lin’s final action · Lin’s route points · Chicago–New Orleans ticket · Subtotal of these two components
Spend two blue and claim Saint Louis–Little Rock · 6 + 2 = 8 · Connected: +7 · 15
Draw train cards; the map stays unchanged · 6 · Unconnected: −7 · −1

The difference is 16: two points from the short route and fourteen from changing that ticket’s outcome from minus seven to plus seven. We are not relabeling the ticket as having a fourteen-point face value; we are comparing failure with completion. Lin’s other tickets are excluded from the table, so these are not complete final scores and do not establish a winner. Jo’s continuous 44 trains exceed Lin’s maximum of seven, so Jo receives the longest-path bonus in both branches.

This does not show that every short route is more important than a long one. If another path already completed the ticket, those two spaces would not change its scoring again. If two separate routes were still missing, even two cheap claims could not both fit into one remaining action.

The prototype lesson is that inventory does not equal opportunity. Lin still has 40 trains and enough cards, but “draw now, build next time” cannot extend beyond the ending. Write an ending condition as an actual sequence, then play through the triggering player’s action, everyone’s remaining actions, and scoring. Check whether that sequence provides the recovery window you intended.
Follow the designer’s actual development process

In a retrospective co-written with Mark Kaufmann, Moon describes outlining rules and a map, testing alone that day, testing with friends several days later, and adjusting routes, rules, and tickets over subsequent weeks. Kaufmann separately describes publication work on the period setting and title. These are participants’ recollections; they do not establish the specific intention behind each route. The History of Ticket To Ride, printed pp. 6–7.

Our practical proposal is to record each map change alongside the objectives it makes easier or harder. Separately record how naming, images, and historical setting affect understanding. Mechanical and presentation changes can support each other, but require different evidence. Testers wanting another play is useful feedback; it still does not establish balance for every route, ticket, or player count.
Check your understanding
In a two-player game, Jo claims one Dallas–Houston gray route. Can Lin claim the other? No. Only with four or five players can different players use both lanes.
Lin takes red, revealing a locomotive in its place. Can that become the second card? No. A blindly drawn locomotive, however, still counts as one card.
Why does assembling six cards for a black payment not reserve Los Angeles–El Paso? Drawing and claiming are separate turns; Jo may claim first.
Why does the last example’s two-point route change the tracked subtotal by 16? Two points come from the route; fourteen come from moving the ticket from −7 to +7.
Does Jo ending a turn with three trains trigger the ending? No. The threshold is zero, one, or two, and the triggering player also receives one final turn.
Sources and scope

Days of Wonder: 2015 English rules. All four pages checked. The component illustration on p. 2 shows Chicago–New Orleans 7; the map across pp. 2–3 supplies cities, colors, and lengths. Page 3 covers drawing, claiming, and player-count restrictions; p. 4 covers route points, tickets, and ending. Only the base USA map is used.
Days of Wonder: official Ticket to Ride page. Designer identity and old/new rule links; the current component list does not replace the 2015 list.

Alan R. Moon and Mark Kaufmann: The History of Ticket To Ride. Game Trade Magazine, April 2014, printed pp. 6–7, appearing on pp. 5–6 of this public sample PDF. We use the named participants’ accounts of the original design and presentation, not the anniversary-product advertisement as rules evidence.
Modern Art：一幅画的成交价，为什么不是它的价值？
林刚以18卖出一幅画。这个数字看起来很明确，却还不能告诉我们谁赚了多少：钱去了哪里？谁拿到画？轮末这位画家能排第几？《Modern Art》适合用来学习把这些问题分开，再观察它们如何互相影响。
本文采用 CMON 当前提供的英文基础规则，四人、不含 Mystery Player 变体；作者为 Reiner Knizia，见出版社页面。金额沿用该版游戏单位，1代表一千美元。下文是三组本站构造的独立比较，公开各人的现金是为了核算；实际游玩时现金藏在屏风后。这些不是完整对局、最优策略或作者开发记录。
为缩短表格，M、S、D、R、F 分别表示 Manuel Carvalho、Sigrid Thaler、Daniel Melim、Ramon Martins、Rafael Silveira，顺序也是版图从左到右的顺序。
角度一：同样付18，钱流向对手还是银行？
先只看一笔交易。林、乔、梅、博各有100，依次顺时针就座。林拿出一张定价拍卖牌，报18。设这次出牌不结束本轮；我们比较乔立即接手，与乔、梅、博全都放弃两种回应。按定价拍卖与付款规则，PDF第3页，第一条路径由乔付林18；第二条由林付银行18。林必须有能力承担自己报出的价格。
回应 · 成交后林的现金 · 成交后乔的现金 · 谁取得这幅画 · 两人现金合计
三人都放弃，林接手 · 82 · 100 · 林 · 182
现在人为固定一个后续条件：这幅画轮末的结算价值是30，且只统计这笔交易及这幅画的结算贡献。第一条路径变成林118、乔112；第二条变成林112、乔100。梅、博在这段计算中不变，其他交易不计入。
乔在第一条路径上确实净增12，但林净增18。买家“有利润”与“比卖家获益更多”不是同一个判断；林自己接手时则净增12，另有18暂时离开玩家手中的现金池。价格相同，也没有得到同样的对手资金状况。
这里的30是条件，不是林出价时掌握的保证。若实际结算为0，第一条路径乔会损失18，第二条路径由林承担这18。于是定价同时要求林判断别人的接受意愿，以及无人接受时自己能否承受结果。做原创拍卖机制时，可以沿用这个检查方法：先画付款箭头，再算资产收益；不要只写“最高价者获胜”。
这个例子也提醒我们区分手中待出售的牌与已经买下的资产。把林拿出来的牌直接记作“林已经拥有、价值30的收藏”，会把两种不同状态混在一起，使收支表从第一行就算错。
角度二：放弃一次成交，可能保住已经买下的画
换到第一轮的一个局部快照。林准备行动，随后是乔、梅、博。已买下的画与现金如下，桌面累计为 M4、S4、D3、R1、F0。各人仍有手牌；林手中包括一张M和一张D定价牌，乔有一张S。没有双重拍卖悬而未决。
玩家 · 已买下的画 · 当前现金
林 · M两幅、R一幅 · 97
乔 · S两幅、D一幅 · 97
梅 · M两幅、S两幅 · 96
博 · D两幅 · 99
本段用到的规则是：同一画家第五张出场会结束本轮，这张不成交，却参加数量排名；第一轮前三名每幅分别结算30、20、10，其余为0，并列时版图偏左者优先。PDF第4页
林有两条路径。A：现在打出M，直接结束本轮。B：打出D定价牌报8；约定乔、梅放弃，博购买；随后乔打出S，结束本轮。这里把其他人的回应固定下来，方便比较，并不宣称他们必然这样行动。
路径 · 本轮最终出场数：M／S／D／R／F · 前三名 · 林新收到的成交款 · 林轮末卖画收入
B中M与D都是四张，但M位于D左边，因此M排第二。两条路径的新状态可完整结算为：
玩家 · A结算后现金 · B结算后现金 · B比A多／少
林在B多收8，却因自己两幅M各少结算10，最终少12。乔没有买林的D，却因两幅S升值多20；博接下D后多2。选择什么时候停止市场，会重新分配桌上已有资产的收益。
这解释了为什么“再多卖一幅”不能单独当作好行动。设计者可以问：触发结束的动作，除了失去本次交易，还改变了哪些已经投入的资源？若把第五张改成先成交再结束，将会增加一件可结算资产和一次付款；这已是另一种规则，需要另做比较，不能悄悄塞进A的账本。
本表从指定快照开始，只验证本段行动和结算。它没有展开整副牌的逐张发放与此前竞价；更不代表四轮后的赢家。余下轮次仍会继续改变现金。
角度三：历史积累保留了，当前资格仍可能消失
再看一组独立的三轮市场记录。每行数字包含那张触发结束、没有成交的画。这里考察D的结算条件，不追踪某一玩家的完整拍卖收入。
轮次 · 本轮出场数：M／S／D／R／F · D本轮排名 · D本轮新添价值 · 本轮每幅已买下的D结算多少
第二轮留下的历史10没有被擦掉，却不能在当轮兑现。第三轮重新进入前三后，10才与新添的30共同构成40。跨轮价值与清场规则，PDF第4页
一个容易出错的读法是“同一幅D先值10，跌到0，再涨到40，所以一直持有就行”。本例根本没有这样一幅跨轮持有的画：每轮买下的画结算后离场。跨轮保存的是画家的价值记录，以及玩家尚未拿出来拍卖的手牌。若林每轮都买到一幅D，那么三轮收入可以分别是10、0、40，但对应的是三幅不同的画，购买成本还要另外扣除。
这给设计者提供了两个可以分开调节的东西：历史是否保留；当前是否需要重新取得兑现资格。假设某个原创游戏改成“历史奖励永远可领取”，就取消了第二个条件。它可能使先期积累更稳定，也可能使后面的竞争更难影响领先者；这些是待测试的问题，不能把本例当成哪种方案更好的证明。
画家题材在这里让人容易使用“热门”“身价”等词，但玩家还需要知道具体是哪一种数量触发了规则。把出场数量、已购数量和历史价值分别记下来，比笼统说“市场看好D”更能解释下一步会发生什么。它也不等于现实艺术市场的模型或事实判断。
带答案的自查
报18且无人接手，林能否把价格撤回？本例不能；必须承担报出的18。因此要先检查自己的现金。
A里的第五张M算不算林的新收入来源？不算。它影响排名，但没有成为谁买下的画。
B里林收到8，为什么最终反而少12？已有两幅M合计少结算20，减去新收8，净少12。
第三轮D结算40，能否把第二轮已经丢弃的D拿回来再卖？不能。历史价值留在记录上，旧资产已离场。
第二组表能否证明林该在所有对局中立即结束本轮？不能。它固定了资产分布、回应和第一轮条件，只支持这一段比较。
版本与来源
CMON：Modern Art 产品与规则入口：作者、基础产品与牌组数量；本文不采用其他发行版的画家名称。
CMON 英文 Rulebook / Artbook，文件 v18：PDF第2页起始状态、金额单位与组件；第3页付款和定价；第4页结束、并列、清场及跨轮结算；第5页版图顺序与四轮胜负。定位使用PDF页序，不将上传路径年份当作印刷版次。三个算例与设计分析均为本站原创，不复现规则书示例。
Modern Art: Why Is a Painting’s Price Not Its Value?

Lin has just sold a painting for 18. The number looks precise, but it does not tell us who gained how much. Where did the money go? Who acquired the painting? Where will its artist rank when the round ends? Modern Art helps us separate those questions before reconnecting them.

We use CMON’s currently linked English base rules, with four players and no Mystery Player variant. Reiner Knizia is the designer; see the publisher’s page. Amounts use this edition’s game units: 1 represents a thousand dollars. The three independent comparisons below are our constructions. Cash is disclosed for calculation, although players hide it during play. These are neither complete games, optimal strategies, nor accounts of the designer’s development process.
To keep tables readable, M, S, D, R and F stand for Manuel Carvalho, Sigrid Thaler, Daniel Melim, Ramon Martins and Rafael Silveira, in the board’s left-to-right order.
Angle one: Paying 18 to a rival is different from paying 18 to the bank

Start with one transaction. Lin, Jo, Mei and Bo each have 100 and sit in that clockwise order. Lin offers a fixed-price painting for 18. Assume this play does not end the round. Compare Jo accepting immediately with Jo, Mei and Bo all declining. Under the payment and fixed-price rules, PDF p.3, Jo pays Lin in the first branch; Lin pays the bank in the second. Lin must be able to cover the announced price.
Response · Lin’s cash after purchase · Jo’s cash after purchase · Painting acquired by · Their combined cash
Jo buys · 118 · 82 · Jo · 200
All three decline; Lin buys · 82 · 100 · Lin · 182

Now impose one later condition: the painting pays 30 at settlement. Count only this transaction and this painting’s payout. Branch one leaves Lin with 118 and Jo with 112; branch two leaves Lin with 112 and Jo with 100. Mei and Bo are unchanged in this calculation; other transactions are excluded.

Jo genuinely gains 12 in the first branch, but Lin gains 18. A profitable purchase is not automatically a larger gain than the seller’s. Buying it personally gives Lin a gain of 12 instead, and temporarily removes 18 from the cash held by players. An identical price has produced a different distribution of spending power.

The later 30 is a condition, not something Lin is guaranteed when naming a price. If the payout is actually zero, Jo loses 18 in the first branch and Lin bears that loss in the second. Naming a price therefore combines a prediction about acceptance with responsibility for rejection. For an original auction design, draw the payment arrows before calculating asset returns. “The highest bidder wins” leaves too much unexplained.

Also keep a card offered from a hand separate from an asset already purchased. Entering Lin’s offered card in the ledger as “Lin’s collection, already worth 30” confuses two states and corrupts the comparison from its first line.
Angle two: Forgoing a sale can protect paintings already purchased

Move to an independent first-round snapshot. Lin is about to act, followed by Jo, Mei and Bo. Purchased paintings and cash are shown below. The table contains M4, S4, D3, R1 and F0. Everyone still has cards; Lin’s hand includes an M and a fixed-price D, and Jo has an S. No double auction is pending.
Player · Paintings purchased · Current cash
Lin · Two M, one R · 97
Jo · Two S, one D · 97
Mei · Two M, two S · 96
Bo · Two D · 99

The relevant rule: an artist’s fifth appearance ends the round. That card is unbought but counts in the ranking. First-round payouts are 30, 20 and 10 per painting for the top three artists, zero otherwise; ties favor the artist further left on the board. PDF p.4

Lin compares two paths. A: play M now and end the round. B: offer the fixed-price D for 8; stipulate that Jo and Mei pass and Bo buys; Jo then plays S to end the round. Those responses are fixed for comparison, not predictions that the other players must behave this way.
Path · Final appearances: M / S / D / R / F · Top three · New sale proceeds for Lin · Lin’s settlement income
A: M reaches five first · 5 / 4 / 3 / 1 / 0 · M, S, D · 0 · 2 × 30 + 0 = 60
B: D sells; S then reaches five · 4 / 5 / 4 / 1 / 0 · S, M, D · 8 · 2 × 20 + 0 = 40
In B, M and D both have four appearances; M is further left and therefore ranks second. The resulting cash can be settled completely for this segment:
Player · Cash after A · Cash after B · B minus A

Lin receives an extra 8 in B, but the two M paintings each lose 10 of payout, leaving Lin down 12. Jo does not buy Lin’s D yet gains 20 from the two S paintings. Bo’s purchase leaves Bo up 2. Choosing when to stop the market redistributes returns on assets already sitting on the table.

“Sell one more painting” is therefore an incomplete description of a good action. A designer can ask what an ending trigger does to resources committed earlier, alongside the transaction it prevents. Changing the fifth card to sell before ending the round would add both a payment and a payable asset. That is another rule requiring another comparison; it cannot silently enter A’s ledger.

The table starts from a specified snapshot and checks the actions and settlement shown. It does not enumerate a full physical deal or earlier auctions, nor identify the winner after four rounds. Later rounds will continue changing cash.
Angle three: History can remain while current eligibility disappears
Consider a separate three-round market record. Each row includes the unbought card that triggered the ending. We track D’s payout conditions, not a player’s complete auction income.
Round · Appearances: M / S / D / R / F · D’s rank this round · New value added for D · Payout per purchased D this round

The earlier 10 survives round two but cannot pay out in that round. Returning to the top three in round three makes it contribute alongside the new 30. Value across rounds and clearing purchased paintings, PDF p.4

An easy mistake is to read this as “hold the same D while its value moves from 10 to zero to 40.” No such continuously held painting exists here: purchased paintings leave after each settlement. The artist’s value record and cards not yet offered from hands persist instead. If Lin buys one D each round, the receipts can be 10, zero and 40, but they come from three different paintings, with purchase costs still to deduct.

This offers two independently adjustable design questions: does past achievement persist, and must players qualify again to redeem it? Suppose an original game makes historical rewards payable forever. That removes the second condition. Early accumulation might become more reliable, while later competition might find it harder to affect the leader. These are questions to test, not conclusions that this example proves one system superior.

The art setting invites words such as “popular” and “valuable,” but a player still needs to know exactly which count activates a rule. Separate appearances, purchases and historical value before explaining the next action. “The market likes D” conceals those distinctions. Nor should this constructed market be treated as evidence about real art markets.
Check your understanding
Can Lin withdraw the price of 18 after everyone declines? Not here: Lin must cover that price. Check available cash before announcing it.
Does A’s fifth M become another source of income for Lin? No. It changes the ranking without becoming a purchased painting.
Why is Lin down 12 in B despite receiving 8? The two earlier M paintings lose 20 of combined payout; the extra 8 offsets only part of it.
Can a discarded round-two D return for another payment when D pays 40 in round three? No. Historical value persists; the old asset has left.
Does the second comparison prove that Lin should always end a round immediately? No. Its holdings, responses and first-round conditions are fixed; it supports that segment alone.
Edition and sources
CMON: Modern Art product and rules entry: designer, base product and card quantities. Artist names from other editions are not substituted.

The Crew：为什么赢下一墩，反而会让全队失败？
在《The Crew: The Quest for Planet Nine》中，大牌既能拿走目标，也能把目标从需要它的队友面前抢走。设计合作游戏时，不能只把个人分数相加；还要检查胜利由谁取得、别人能知道什么，以及成功发生的次序。

本文采用 Thames & Kosmos 英文基础规则，产品691868、文件内码691868-02-060320，不使用《Mission Deep Sea》。三个独立例子都是本站构造的合法发牌与行动路线，不是规则书例题或真人试玩。均为四人，顺时针甲→乙→丙→丁；不开求救信号，无额外沟通限制。每例从发牌后开始，甲持火箭4，先选任务并首攻。小任务牌不计入40张出牌；蓝、绿、黄、粉各有1—9，另有火箭1—4。规则第2、8—10页
下表向读者展示全手牌以便复算；游戏中的队员只能看自己手牌、公开任务及合法公开的信息，不能照着全知表讨论。已经收走的牌墩也不是随时可翻的公共档案：规则只允许查看最近一墩。表内“蓝8、9”表示蓝8和蓝9，各表每行恰好十张。
角度一：合作目标改变的是大牌的用途
采用真实任务2：两张任务牌，没有顺序标记。此次抽出蓝2与绿3，甲先取蓝2，乙取绿3。日志PDF第3页左栏任务2，印刷第4页
队员 · 完整初始手牌
第一墩依次出甲绿2、乙绿7、丙绿3。现在轮到丁，他有三张绿牌，必须跟绿，不能打火箭3；但没有必须压过绿7的义务。跟牌与火箭见规则第3—4页
丁出绿1：乙的绿7最大，乙收下四张牌，包括自己任务要求的绿3；乙翻面该任务。
从同一选择点改出绿9：丁收下绿3，拿到它的却不是任务持有人乙，整次任务尝试立即失败。不能再打几墩补救。任务结算见规则第10页
继续绿1的分支。乙赢了上一墩，所以由乙首攻：乙蓝2→丙蓝4→丁蓝6→甲蓝9。四人都有蓝牌，出牌合法；甲拿到蓝2，第二张任务完成，全队成功，立即结束。共收走8张，四人各余8张，合计32张，不需要把它们打完。
这里，丁放弃一次取墩帮助乙完成任务，乙再把蓝2送进甲能赢的墩。两人的作用不能用“各赢几墩”排序。任务把牌的价值连接到特定接收者，大牌保留在谁手里，也就改变了下一步协作。
这条路线证明的是所列行动可以成功，不能证明队员在隐蔽信息下必然找到它，也不能推出丁永远应该留大牌。任务归属、剩余花色或先手改变后，同一张绿9可能正是救场的牌。
角度二：公开一张牌，同时规定它能说什么
另开一次任务2，甲先取绿2，乙取黄4。完整发牌如下，乙尚未使用沟通：
队员 · 完整初始手牌
任务分好、第一墩尚未开始时，乙把黄7亮在面前，绿色沟通标记放顶部，表示它是自己最大的黄牌；再拿提示牌入手。黄7仍是可出的第十张牌，提示牌不是额外的出牌。乙此时还持黄1，不能把标记放中间宣称“唯一”。规则第5—7页的沟通文字与组件图
沿下面路线逐墩结算；箭头顺序就是出牌顺序：
墩 · 出牌与结算
1 · 甲黄9→乙黄1→丙黄2→丁黄3。甲收牌，没有目标牌；乙剩9张可出牌，含桌上的黄7。
2 · 甲黄5→乙黄7→丙黄4→丁黄6。乙收下黄4，完成自己的任务；黄7打出，提示牌移出手中，沟通标记翻红。
3 · 乙绿1→丙绿2→丁绿3→甲绿9。甲完成绿2，全队成功。每人余7张，共28张，另有12张已收走。
第一墩之后，黄7成为乙唯一的黄牌，顶部标记仍不能搬到中间。第二墩打出它以后，乙也不能再沟通另一张牌：沟通额度是每人每次任务尝试一次，只能在一墩开始前使用，第一墩前也可以。标记保留的是那次声明，没有持续更新整副手牌。规则第5、7页
这个信号确实排除了“乙还有黄8或黄9”，却没有承诺黄7将赢。第二墩的丁仍有黄8；若改打黄8，黄4会落到丁面前，任务失败。乙不能通过标记传达一整套未来出牌指令，其他人也不能从一次声明读出未公开的所有牌。
对初学设计者，这里值得分别检查“允许公开什么”“何时公开”“信息是否更新”。桌面上的黄7降低了记忆负担，提示牌提醒它仍待出，红面则记录额度已用。这些物件承担不同工作。是否真的让某组新手更轻松，需要观察他们使用组件时的错误，本文没有测量这种效果。
角度三：先完成的目标，不一定出现在第一墩
第三次采用真实任务3：两张任务牌，附数字1、2。这次按抽出顺序将粉2配1、蓝3配2；甲先选粉2及其标记，乙取蓝3及其标记。任务1必须先于任务2完成；这里的数字不是墩数。日志PDF第3页左栏任务3，印刷第4页；规则第14—16页
队员 · 完整初始手牌
甲先出火箭4，乙、丙、丁依次跟火箭1、2、3。甲赢下第一墩，没有完成任何目标，但也没有违反次序。四枚火箭全部离场，余36张。
甲继续首攻粉9，乙粉1、丙粉2、丁粉3跟出，甲取得标记1的粉2。第三墩甲出蓝1，乙蓝9、丙蓝3、丁蓝4跟出，乙取得标记2的蓝3。任务按1→2完成，全队成功；桌外已收12张，四人各余7张。
现在回到第一墩结束时，保持发牌不变，只把第二墩换成甲蓝1→乙蓝9→丙蓝3→丁蓝4。乙虽然是蓝3的正确接收者，标记1的粉2却尚未完成，因此立即失败。不能声称“反正第三墩能补粉2”，先后条件检查的是发生过的过程。
这说明任务除了指定终点，还能规定抵达路线。没有目标的第一墩仍可能改变后续条件：本例清掉了四枚火箭，并保留甲的先手。我们没有据此证明开火箭4最优。另须注意，本例两张任务属于不同人，才必然要由不同墩完成；不能扩写成所有带顺序标记的任务都必须分墩，规则另有同一人同墩完成连续标记的情况。
作者亲述与本站分析
Thomas Sing 在 IELLO 于2021年3月1日转载的访谈中回忆：他先想到预先指定谁赢哪张牌，次日拿去测试；当晚沟通尚未完善，下一周才带来后来采用的沟通规则。太空主题是数周后才加入的。访谈“Acte 1 : de l’idée au prototype”
以上是作者对开发过程的回忆。本文从中得到的练习建议是：先测试“接收者改变后，出牌是否产生合作需要”，再单独测试信息规则如何影响决定。它不是作者提供的通用设计方法，也不能把他对早期原型的评价当作本文三个例子已通过玩家验证。
带答案的自查
角度一中，丁为何不能用火箭3，又为何可以出绿1？丁仍有绿牌，必须跟绿；跟牌不等于必须赢墩。
角度一结束时，为什么还有32张没打也算成功？两张任务已经由各自持有人完成；成功不要求清空手牌。
角度二第一墩后，能把黄7的标记移到中间吗？不能；黄7虽成唯一黄牌，原沟通标记的位置不能更新。
“乙最大的黄牌是7”能保证第二墩乙赢吗？不能，丁仍有黄8；本路线中丁选择了黄6。
角度三第一墩没完成标记1，为什么不失败？数字规定任务之间的完成顺序，不规定在哪一墩完成。
版本与来源

The Crew: Why Can Winning a Trick Make the Whole Team Lose?

In The Crew: The Quest for Planet Nine, a high card can secure a target or take it away from the teammate who needs it. Designing cooperation involves more than adding individual scores together. Who receives a success, what others can know, and when success happens all matter.

This article uses the Thames & Kosmos English base rules, product 691868, document code 691868-02-060320, excluding Mission Deep Sea. The three independent deals and action sequences below are our original constructions, not rulebook exercises or observed playtests. All use four players, clockwise A→B→C→D, without a distress signal or additional communication restrictions. Each begins after dealing. A holds rocket 4, chooses a task first, and leads the opening trick. Small task cards are separate from the 40 playing cards: blue, green, yellow, and pink each run from 1 to 9, plus rockets 1–4. Rules, pp.2, 8–10

The full hands let readers verify the arithmetic. At the table, players see their own hands, public tasks, and information legally made public; they cannot discuss these all-seeing tables. Captured tricks are not a freely searchable archive either: only the most recent trick may be inspected. In each table, “blue 8, 9” means two separate blue cards. Every row contains exactly ten playing cards.
Angle one: A cooperative objective changes what a high card is for
Use published mission 2: two tasks without order tokens. This attempt draws blue 2 and green 3. A selects blue 2 first; B takes green 3. Logbook PDF p.3, left-hand mission 2, printed p.4
Player · Complete starting hand
A · Rocket 4; blue 8, 9; green 2; yellow 1, 4, 7; pink 2, 5, 8
B · Rocket 1; blue 2, 5; green 4, 7; yellow 2, 5; pink 3, 6, 9
C · Rocket 2; blue 1, 4; green 3, 5, 6; yellow 3, 6; pink 1, 4
D · Rocket 3; blue 3, 6, 7; green 1, 8, 9; yellow 8, 9; pink 7
The first trick begins A green 2→B green 7→C green 3. D now has three greens and must follow green; rocket 3 is unavailable. D is not obliged to beat green 7. Following suit and rockets, rules pp.3–4
D plays green 1: B's green 7 wins all four cards, including B's required green 3. B turns that task face down.
Return to the same decision and choose green 9: D captures green 3 instead of its task owner B. The mission attempt fails immediately; later tricks cannot repair it. Task resolution, rules p.10

Continue the green-1 branch. B won the previous trick and therefore leads: B blue 2→C blue 4→D blue 6→A blue 9. Everyone has blue and follows legally. A captures blue 2, completing the second task. The team succeeds and stops immediately. Eight cards have been captured; each player has eight left, totaling 32. They need not play those remaining cards.

D gives up a trick to help B complete a task; B then puts blue 2 into a trick A can win. Ranking their contributions by tricks won would miss their relationship. The task connects a card's value to a particular recipient, while the location of retained high cards changes the next opportunity for cooperation.

This sequence establishes that the stated actions can succeed. It does not establish that players will discover them with hidden information, or that D should always save high cards. Change task ownership, remaining suits, or the leader, and green 9 might be exactly the card that saves the attempt.
Angle two: Revealing a card also restricts what it can say
Start another attempt at mission 2. A chooses green 2 first; B takes yellow 4. Here is the complete new deal, with B's communication still unused:
Player · Complete starting hand
A · Rocket 4; blue 2, 5; green 6, 9; yellow 5, 9; pink 1, 4, 7
B · Rockets 1, 2; blue 1, 4; green 1, 4; yellow 1, 7; pink 3, 6
C · Blue 3, 6; green 2, 5, 8; yellow 2, 4; pink 2, 5, 8
D · Rocket 3; blue 7, 8, 9; green 3, 7; yellow 3, 6, 8; pink 9

After distributing tasks but before the opening trick, B displays yellow 7 with the green communication token at its top, identifying B's highest yellow, and takes a reminder card. Yellow 7 remains the tenth playable card; the reminder supplies no extra play. Because B also holds yellow 1, placing the token in the middle to claim “only yellow” would be false. Communication text and component diagrams, rules pp.5–7
Follow this route. Arrows show the actual order of play:
Trick · Plays and resolution
1 · A yellow 9→B yellow 1→C yellow 2→D yellow 3. A wins, with no target captured. B has nine playable cards left, including the displayed yellow 7.
2 · A yellow 5→B yellow 7→C yellow 4→D yellow 6. B captures yellow 4 and completes that task. Playing yellow 7 removes the reminder from B's hand and turns the communication token red.
3 · B green 1→C green 2→D green 3→A green 9. A completes green 2 and the team succeeds. Each player has seven cards left: 28 remaining plus 12 captured.

After trick 1, yellow 7 has become B's only yellow, but the token must stay at the top. After playing it in trick 2, B cannot communicate another card. Communication is limited to once per player per attempt and occurs only before a trick, never during one. The marker preserves the original declaration; it does not continuously update the whole hand. Rules pp.5, 7

The signal rules out B holding yellow 8 or 9. It does not promise yellow 7 will win. In trick 2, D still holds yellow 8: choosing it instead would send yellow 4 to D and fail the mission. The marker does not let B transmit a complete set of future instructions, and one statement does not expose every uncommunicated card.

A beginning designer can examine three separate questions here: what may be disclosed, when disclosure happens, and whether it updates. The displayed yellow 7 reduces what needs remembering, the reminder points to a card still waiting to be played, and the red face records a spent allowance. These components have different jobs. Establishing whether they make learning easier for a particular group would require observing that group's handling errors; this article contains no such measurement.
Angle three: The first completed task need not happen in the first trick

The third attempt uses published mission 3: two tasks with number tokens 1 and 2. This draw assigns token 1 to pink 2 and token 2 to blue 3. A chooses pink 2 with its token; B takes blue 3 with its token. Task 1 must precede task 2. Those numbers do not identify trick numbers. Logbook PDF p.3, left-hand mission 3, printed p.4; rules pp.14–16
Player · Complete starting hand
A · Rocket 4; blue 1, 8; green 1, 4, 7; yellow 1, 4; pink 6, 9
B · Rocket 1; blue 2, 9; green 2, 5; yellow 2, 5; pink 1, 4, 7
C · Rocket 2; blue 3, 6; green 3, 6; yellow 3, 6; pink 2, 5, 8
D · Rocket 3; blue 4, 5, 7; green 8, 9; yellow 7, 8, 9; pink 3

A opens with rocket 4; B, C, and D follow with rockets 1, 2, and 3. A wins the opening trick. No task is complete, but no ordering condition has been broken. All four rockets have left the hands, leaving 36 playing cards.

A next leads pink 9. B follows pink 1, C pink 2, and D pink 3. A captures pink 2, completing token 1. In trick 3, A plays blue 1, followed by B blue 9, C blue 3, and D blue 4. B captures blue 3, completing token 2. The team succeeds in the required order, 1→2. Twelve cards are captured and each player retains seven.

Now return to the end of the opening trick, preserving the deal. Replace trick 2 with A blue 1→B blue 9→C blue 3→D blue 4. B is the correct recipient of blue 3, but pink 2 with token 1 remains incomplete. The attempt therefore fails immediately. Planning to collect pink 2 later cannot repair a condition checked against the actual sequence.

A task can prescribe a route as well as a destination. An opening trick with no target can still change future conditions: this one removes every rocket while leaving A on lead. That does not prove that leading rocket 4 is optimal. Also, these two tasks require separate tricks because they belong to different players. Do not generalize that all ordered tasks must be separated: the rules also allow one player to complete consecutive order tokens in the same trick.
The designer's account and our analysis

In an interview republished by IELLO on March 1, 2021, Thomas Sing recalled first imagining predetermined recipients for particular cards and testing the idea the following day. Communication was still unfinished that evening; he brought the subsequently adopted communication rule the next week. The space theme followed several weeks later. Interview, “Acte 1 : de l’idée au prototype”

That is the designer's recollection of development. Our proposed exercise is to test whether changing the required recipient creates a need to cooperate, then separately test how information rules affect decisions. This is our inference, not a general design method supplied by Sing. His assessment of his early prototype does not establish that players have tested the three examples here.
Self-checks with answers
Why can D play green 1 but not rocket 3 in angle one? D still has greens and must follow green. Following suit does not require winning.
Why does angle one succeed with 32 cards unplayed? Both tasks have reached their respective owners; empty hands are not required.
May B move yellow 7's marker to the middle after angle two's opening trick? No. Although it is now B's only yellow, the original marker placement cannot update.
Does “B's highest yellow is 7” guarantee that B wins trick 2? No. D still has yellow 8; D chooses yellow 6 in this route.
Why does completing no task in angle three's first trick avoid failure? The numbers specify the order among tasks, not the trick in which each must be completed.
Edition and sources

Azul：拿到的砖，为什么不等于这轮得到的分？
同样拿一块砖，它可能补完一条模式线，接通墙上的两段图案，也可能落到地板上。本文用三个独立局面，分别观察公共供给、分阶段结算与终局时机怎样改变一次选择。
范围固定为 Michael Kiesling 的原版《Azul》，采用出版社所链接、版权页标注 ©2018 Plan B Games 的六页英文基础规则，双方都用彩墙面。Summer Pavilion、Stained Glass、Mini、扩展及灰墙变体均不在本文范围。局面与设计分析为本站原创，不是作者试玩记录。
以下始终是林、乔两人，轮流行动。“第几线”指左边容量为1至5的模式线；“行、列”指右边墙格，从上往下、从左往右数。蓝、黄、红、黑、白分别简写为 B、Y、R、K、W；白指白底花纹砖。彩墙五行的固定颜色依次是 BYRKW、WBYRK、KWBYR、RKWBY、YRKWB。组件与板面见规则第2页。
角度一：你留下的砖，会组成别人的下一组选项
第一轮，双方0分，墙、模式线和地板全空；林先手，起始标记放中央。五个工厂的全部砖为：F1＝BBRR，F2＝BBYY，F3＝KKKK，F4＝WWWW，F5＝YYYY。中央没有彩砖，袋里余80块，盒盖为空。
林先从F1取全部2蓝放第2线，把2红推入中央；乔从F2取全部2蓝放第2线，把2黄也推入中央。现在中央是2红、2黄和标记。接下来比较两组明确写定的回应：
行动者 · 甲：林现在取中央红 · 乙：林先拿白
林 · 中央2红：第1线放1红，另1红落地，同时拿标记 · F4的4白放第4线
乔 · F3的4黑放第4线 · 中央2红：第1线放1红，另1红落地，同时拿标记
林 · F4的4白放第4线 · F3的4黑放第5线
乔 · F5的4黄放第5线 · F5的4黄放第4线
林 · 中央全部2黄放第3线 · 中央全部2黄放第3线
工厂与中央至此全空。甲中林移上墙的红、蓝、白彼此不相邻，各得1分；地板有标记和红砖，扣1＋1，得分为3－2＝1。乔的蓝、黑各得1分，合计2。乙中林的蓝、白各1分，合计2；乔的红、蓝、黄各1分，扣标记与红砖的2分后剩1。两边都未触发终局。取砖、溢出与结算，规则第3—5页
甲保留林第3线的2黄、乔第5线的4黄；乙保留林第3线的2黄及第5线的4黑，乔没有未完成线。完成线只移一砖上墙，余砖与落地彩砖收进盒盖。甲下一轮林先手，乙乔先手；都从仍有80块的袋中补满五个工厂，不能立即回收盒盖来挑颜色。
林不能只取中央1红，也不能把取来的2红分放第1、3线。一个选择因此同时改变自己的承接容量、公共区余砖和下轮先手。上表指定了乔的回应，所以1比2不是必然胜负；它展示的是：等待可能让另一人先拿走那一组砖。公共区并不是替你保管的仓库。
角度二：补满一条线，可能同时改变后面一块砖的分数
换一个中后盘切片：五工厂全空，中央只剩1黑，轮到林。林3分，墙上仅有（2,1）白、（2,3）黄、（3,2）白；模式线依次为1黄、2蓝、2黑、4红、第5线空；地板只有起始标记。乔0分、空墙，第5线有4红，其他线空；地板前六格各有1黄。
本例与下一例都明确给出切片的供给：袋中每色4块，其余未摆出的彩砖均在盒盖；没有其他桌面砖。它们不复原此前每轮抽取历史。未列出的墙格均为空。
林取最后1黑，有两个合法去处。把它补进第3线，按从上往下的顺序，结算如下：
移上墙的位置 · 此刻连在一起的砖 · 得分
第1行第2列，黄 · 尚无直接邻砖 · 1
第2行第2列，蓝 · 横向白—蓝—黄3块；纵向黄—蓝—白3块 · 3＋3＝6
第3行第1列，黑 · 横向黑—白2块；纵向白—黑2块 · 2＋2＝4
第4行第1列，红 · 纵向白—黑—红3块 · 3
林得3＋1＋6＋4＋3－1＝16分，模式线全清空。第二个过程是主动把最后1黑放地板：第3线仍只有2黑，不上墙；其他三块依次得1、6、1分。第4行的红上方有空格，所以不能跨空格连接第2行的白。林得3＋1＋6＋1－2＝9分，并保留第3线的2黑。两边乔均保留4红，地板扣11但最低为0分；无人结束游戏，林拿回标记并负责下一轮补砖。模式线保留、顺序与横竖计分，规则第4—5页
这1黑带来的7分差额，是黑砖的4分、后续红砖多出的2分，以及少扣的1分共同组成。横竖同时连接时，新砖在两条连续线上各算一次；对角接触则不算。先结算第2线再回头补第1线，会漏掉刚放上的黄砖，不能这样改变顺序。
这不是“长线永远更好”。本例能产生连锁，是因为墙上已经有指定邻砖，而且第4线也已完成。设计一个先积累、再兑现的系统时，要同时检查完成条件与兑现顺序；只比较收了几块，会漏掉它们怎样互相增值。
角度三：结束时点，决定已完成的目标何时兑现
再换一个局面，林26分、乔6分，五工厂全空、中央只剩1白，轮到林。双方墙上的全部砖如下；点号代表空位，不代表可任选颜色。
墙行 · 林 · 乔
林第1线空，第2至5线依次有1蓝、2黄、3黑、4红，地板空；乔第2线1黄、第4线3红、第5线5蓝，其余线空，地板只有标记。取最后1白后，林比较完成第1线，或让白砖落地。不能改放第2至5线：对应墙行已经各有一块白。
完成第1线时，白砖进入（1,5），横向5块、纵向5块，立即得10分。林完成了一整横行，但乔仍要把第5线的蓝移到（5,5），与左侧白连接得2分，再扣标记1分。双方先到36与7分，整个铺墙阶段结束后才进入终局奖励。林的一横行、一竖列、五块白共加2＋7＋10＝19，最终55分；乔集齐五块蓝，加10，最终17分。游戏结束，不补工厂。终局与奖励，规则第6页
若林把白放地板，这轮没有新墙砖，扣1后为25分；乔仍结算到7分。虽然乔已有五块蓝，但双方都没有完整横行，因此此时不加那10分，游戏继续。乔持标记，下一轮从袋内20块补出五个四砖工厂；抽出的分组未指定，不能预先算入后续得分。最后白砖在此分支回到盒盖。两边未满的模式线均保留；结束分支不再有补完它们的机会。
这里比较的是“现在结算后的状态”，不能拿55比25宣称前一分支整局一定更好：后一分支还有未来行动。这个局面揭示了两个不同条件：完整横行负责触发结束，横行、竖列与集齐颜色负责终局奖励。触发者也不能取消别人的本轮铺墙。设计自己的目标时，把“得到奖励”和“停止继续行动”分开写，才能检查玩家究竟控制了什么。
设计者记录：余砖的去向曾经改变过
在2018年7月31日的 Brettspielbox 访谈中，Kiesling 回顾，一家出版社退回作品并提供反馈；早期砖块原本顺时针传递，他后来改为把砖推入中央。他把这次修改放在吸收外界批评的开发经历中讲述。
这支持“传递关系确实改过”，不支持本文七步过程是作者的实验，也不能凭访谈计算改版提高了多少乐趣。本站从角度一提出的分析是：改变余砖去向，也改变了谁能在下一次行动选择它们。要进一步比较旧机制与新机制，还需要明确原型细节并实际试玩。
带答案的自查
角度一取2红，只缺1红，能把另一块另放一条线吗？不能。该次选择只能进入一条模式线，溢出进地板。
角度二蓝砖为什么得6而非5？横向3与纵向3分别计分，交点的新砖分别包含在两次计数里。
角度二把最后黑砖落地，第3线的2黑会被清走吗？不会。未完成线保留；红砖也因此只得1分。
角度三林完成横行后，乔的5蓝还能上墙吗？能。整个铺墙阶段做完，才结算终局奖励。
只完成竖列或五块同色会结束吗？不会。后一分支乔的五蓝也不会立刻加10分。
地板前3格都有物件，扣多少？1＋1＋2＝4；若铺墙后只有2分，就降到0而不是负2。七格全满时再落下的彩砖进入盒盖，不新增扣分格。规则第4—5页

Azul: Why Do Tiles Taken Not Equal Points Earned This Round?

A single tile might complete a pattern line, connect two sections of a wall, or fall to the floor. Three independent situations examine how shared supplies, staged resolution and the timing of the ending change a choice.

This article uses Michael Kiesling’s original Azul, with both players using the colored wall. Our fixed reference is the six-page English base rulebook, bearing ©2018 Plan B Games, linked by the publisher. Summer Pavilion, Stained Glass, Mini, expansions and the gray-wall variant are outside this article. The situations and design analysis are ours, not the designer’s playtest records.

Every example has two players, Lin and Jo, alternating turns. A “pattern line” is on the left, with capacities one through five. Wall rows run top to bottom and columns left to right. B, Y, R, K and W mean blue, yellow, red, black and white; white identifies the patterned tile with a white background. The colored wall’s five rows are BYRKW, WBYRK, KWBYR, RKWBY and YRKWB. Components and board: rules page 2.
Angle one: What you leave becomes somebody else’s next set of options

It is round one. Both players have zero points and empty walls, pattern lines and floors. Lin starts, placing the starting player marker in the center. The five factories contain all of these tiles: F1 = BBRR, F2 = BBYY, F3 = KKKK, F4 = WWWW and F5 = YYYY. There are no colored tiles in the center, eighty remain in the bag, and the box lid is empty.

Lin takes both blues from F1 into pattern line 2, pushing both reds into the center. Jo takes both blues from F2 into line 2 and pushes both yellows into the center. The center now holds two reds, two yellows and the marker. Compare two specified sequences of responses:
Player · A: Lin takes the central reds now · B: Lin takes white first
Lin · Both central reds: one in line 1, one on the floor; also take the marker · F4’s four whites into line 4
Jo · F3’s four blacks into line 4 · Both central reds: one in line 1, one on the floor; also take the marker
Lin · F4’s four whites into line 4 · F3’s four blacks into line 5
Jo · F5’s four yellows into line 5 · F5’s four yellows into line 4
Lin · Both central yellows into line 3 · Both central yellows into line 3

All factories and the center are now empty. In A, Lin moves a red, a blue and a white onto the wall. None is directly adjacent to another, so each scores one. The marker and red tile on the floor cost 1 + 1: Lin has 3 − 2 = 1 point. Jo’s blue and black score one each, totaling two. In B, Lin’s blue and white total two; Jo’s red, blue and yellow total three, reduced by two for the marker and red tile, leaving one. Neither branch ends the game. Taking tiles, overflow and resolution: rules pages 3–5.

A retains Lin’s two yellows in line 3 and Jo’s four yellows in line 5. B retains Lin’s two yellows in line 3 and four blacks in line 5; Jo has no incomplete lines. Each completed line sends just one tile to the wall; its other tiles and fallen colored tiles go into the lid. Lin starts next round in A, Jo in B. Both branches refill five factories from the eighty tiles still in the bag, without immediately recycling the lid to obtain preferred colors.

Lin cannot take just one central red or split those two reds between pattern lines 1 and 3. A choice therefore changes personal capacity, the shared supply and the next starting player together. Jo’s responses are specified, so the scores are not a forced outcome. They demonstrate that waiting can let somebody else take the group first. The shared center does not reserve supplies for you.
Angle two: Completing one line can also increase a later tile’s score

Use a different, later-game snapshot. All five factories are empty, the center holds only one black, and Lin acts next. Lin has three points. The only wall tiles are white at (2,1), yellow at (2,3) and white at (3,2). Pattern lines contain, respectively, one yellow, two blues, two blacks, four reds, and nothing in line 5. Lin’s floor holds only the starting player marker. Jo has zero points, an empty wall, four reds in line 5, no other pattern tiles, and six yellows occupying the first six floor spaces.

This example and the next specify their supplies: four tiles of each color remain in the bag; every colored tile not listed on the table or in the bag is in the box lid. There are no other table tiles. These snapshots do not reconstruct the draws in all earlier rounds. Every unlisted wall space is empty.
Lin takes the last black and compares two legal destinations. Complete pattern line 3, then resolve from top to bottom:
Tile moved to the wall · Connected tiles at that moment · Points
Yellow at row 1, column 2 · No directly adjacent tile yet · 1
Blue at row 2, column 2 · White–blue–yellow horizontally; yellow–blue–white vertically · 3 + 3 = 6
Black at row 3, column 1 · Black–white horizontally; white–black vertically · 2 + 2 = 4
Red at row 4, column 1 · White–black–red vertically · 3

Lin reaches 3 + 1 + 6 + 4 + 3 − 1 = 16 points, with every pattern line cleared. Alternatively, Lin deliberately puts the last black on the floor. Line 3 still has only two blacks and contributes no wall tile. The other three placements score one, six and one. A gap above the new red prevents it connecting to the white in row 2. Lin reaches 3 + 1 + 6 + 1 − 2 = 9 and retains the two blacks in line 3. In both branches Jo retains four reds; the eleven-point floor penalty cannot take Jo below zero. Nobody ends the game; Lin retrieves the marker and prepares the next round. Retention, order and horizontal/vertical scoring: rules pages 4–5.

The seven-point difference combines four from the black placement, two extra from the later red, and one avoided floor penalty. When both directions connect, the new tile belongs to both counted lines; diagonal contact does not count. Resolving line 2 before returning to line 1 would omit the newly placed yellow and is not a permitted change of order.

This does not make longer pattern lines universally better. The effect requires these existing neighbors and an already completed fourth line. In a system that accumulates resources before converting them, examine both the completion requirement and the conversion order. Counting collected pieces alone misses how their values depend on one another.
Angle three: The ending determines when completed goals pay out

Use another position, with Lin on twenty-six points and Jo on six. All five factories are empty. The center contains one white, and Lin acts next. The table shows every tile on both walls. A dot is an empty space, not a free choice of color.
Wall row · Lin · Jo

Lin’s line 1 is empty. Lines 2 through 5 contain one blue, two yellows, three blacks and four reds respectively; the floor is empty. Jo has one yellow in line 2, three reds in line 4 and five blues in line 5, no other pattern tiles, and only the marker on the floor. After taking the last white, Lin can complete line 1 or let the white fall to the floor. Lines 2 through 5 cannot receive it: each corresponding wall row already contains a white.

Complete line 1 and place white at (1,5). It joins five tiles horizontally and five vertically, scoring ten immediately. Lin has completed a horizontal row, but Jo still moves a blue from line 5 to (5,5), scoring two with the white to its left, then loses one for the marker. The scores reach thirty-six and seven. Only after the entire wall-tiling phase do end bonuses apply. Lin’s completed row, completed column and five whites add 2 + 7 + 10 = 19, producing a final score of fifty-five. Jo’s five blues add ten, producing seventeen. The game ends and factories are not refilled. Ending and bonuses: rules page 6.

If Lin puts the white on the floor, Lin adds no wall tile and drops to twenty-five after the one-point penalty. Jo still reaches seven. Jo now has five blues, but neither player has completed a horizontal row: the ten-point bonus is not awarded yet, and play continues. Jo holds the marker and refills five four-tile factories from the twenty tiles in the bag. The random groups are unspecified and cannot be credited with future points. The last white returns to the lid in this branch. Both branches retain the incomplete pattern lines; the ending branch offers no further opportunity to complete them.

We are comparing states after the present resolution. Fifty-five versus twenty-five does not prove that the first branch must be better over the whole game: the second still has future actions. The situation separates two conditions. A completed horizontal row triggers the ending; rows, columns and complete colors determine end bonuses. The player who triggers the ending cannot cancel another player’s wall placements this round. When designing goals, write “award points” and “stop further play” separately to see what players actually control.
Designer’s account: The destination of leftover tiles changed

In the Brettspielbox interview dated July 31, 2018, Kiesling recalls a publisher returning the game with feedback. Tiles originally passed clockwise; he changed this so they went into the center. He describes the revision while discussing the importance of accepting criticism from others.

This supports an actual change to the passing relationship. It does not make our seven-turn sequence the designer’s experiment, or quantify how much enjoyment the revision added. Our inference from angle one is that changing where leftovers go also changes who can select them on a subsequent turn. Comparing the old and new mechanisms further would require the prototype’s actual details and playtesting.
Check your understanding, with answers
In angle one, can Lin place the second red in another pattern line after filling line 1? No. That selection can enter one pattern line; overflow goes to the floor.
Why does angle two’s blue score six rather than five? The horizontal three and vertical three are counted separately, each including the new tile at their intersection.
If the last black falls to the floor in angle two, are the two blacks in line 3 removed? No. The incomplete line remains; the resulting gap also leaves the red scoring only one.
Can Jo still move a blue from the five-blue pattern line after Lin completes a horizontal row? Yes. Finish the entire wall-tiling phase before awarding end bonuses.
Does a completed column or five tiles of one color end the game? No. Jo’s five blues in the continuing branch do not immediately add ten points either.

What do three occupied floor spaces cost? 1 + 1 + 2 = 4. A score of two after wall placements drops to zero, not minus two. If all seven floor spaces are occupied, further fallen colored tiles go into the lid without adding penalty spaces. Rules pages 4–5.

Root：同一张地图，为什么是三种不同的压力？
猫族仓库里有木材，却不能拿来建造；鹰巢有兵力，却可能因为无法兑现一张牌而陷入动荡；森林联盟失去士兵后，仍可能留住影响力。理解《Root》的非对称设计，需要同时看资源在哪里、行动何时必须发生，以及一次冲突还会留下什么。
本文采用《The Law of Root》2025年10月13日版中的基础阵营规则，设计者为 Cole Wehrle，见出版社产品页。以下三个独立片段处于四人基础游戏环境，浪人在片段中不参与；不使用扩展、支配胜利或额外卡牌效果。字母只是空地的临时名称。我们给出本段所需的连接与状态，不重建此前完整对局，也不把它当作新地图或最优策略。
角度一：木材够了，为什么仍然付不了费用？
现在是猫族白昼，还可使用两个行动。猫族有8分，地图上已有三座锯木厂；下一座需3木、得3分，轨道数值可对照Learning to Play 第11页。准备建造的C有一个空建筑位。
三片空地以道路连接为 A—B—C，A与C不直接相邻；其他路线不能提供一条由猫族控制的绕行通路。全图仅有的3木都在A。除表中所列外，这三处没有其他棋子，也没有同情标记。
空地 · 猫族士兵／建筑 · 鹰巢士兵／建筑 · 木材 · 现在由谁控制
B不是猫族控制：士兵加建筑为2对2，鹰巢的平手优势生效。A的3木不能越过B来支付C的建造费用。木材也不参与控制权计算。这里用到的是Law 第2.5、6.5.4、7.2.2节，第3、6页。
比较两条行动路径。A路径现在停手，不建造，状态不变。B路径先用一次行军，把C的一名猫兵移到B；行军允许最多两次移动，此处只做一次。起点C由猫族控制，所以移动合法。B变为猫族2兵加1工坊，对鹰巢2兵；C还剩2猫兵。猫族终于连续控制A、B、C。
随后用第二个行动，在C建锯木厂，移除A的3木支付费用，得3分。这个片段到建造结算结束：
结果 · A木材 · B猫兵／C猫兵 · C新增建筑 · 猫族分数 · 本段使用行动
B：移动，再建造 · 0 · 2／2 · 1座锯木厂 · 11 · 2
这次没有消灭敌兵，也没有多生产木材。改变的是资源的可达性：一名士兵重新分配后，原有库存才成为可支付库存。若只把界面写成“总木材3”，就会漏掉这次决策的核心。
做自己的区域游戏时，可以分别记录总量、可用量和打开通路的行动成本。把木材改成全图共享储备，会取消这个运输条件，也会改变守住B的意义；它不是单纯减少一次搬运操作。本例只说明两种行动的当前结果，不能证明增建锯木厂一定比保留兵力、行动和木材更好。
角度二：一张万能牌，既买灵活性也增加未来责任
换到鹰巢的晨歌。领袖为 Builder；已有政令如下，忠诚宰相都算鸟牌。手中恰有一张狐狸牌和一张鸟牌，均不是伏击或支配牌。我们比较只添加其中一张到建造栏，另一张留手。
政令栏 · 原有牌
招募 · 忠诚宰相鸟牌、狐狸牌
移动 · 忠诚宰相鸟牌、兔子牌
战斗 · 空
建造 · 空；本次加狐狸或鸟
地图上鹰巢仅有两座鸟巢：D为狐狸空地，有2鹰兵和1鸟巢；相邻的E为兔子空地，也有2鹰兵和1鸟巢；E另邻接老鼠空地F，F为空且有空建筑位。鹰巢有16名备用士兵、10分。这三处没有敌人、遗迹或其他效果；其他狐狸空地都不受鹰巢控制。省略的地图部分不会提供额外行动目标。
两条路径都不制造卡牌，并执行相同的前两栏：在D招募两次，D从2兵变4兵；先为鸟牌从D移1兵到E，再为兔子牌从E移1兵到F。此时D3兵、E2兵、F1兵，备用兵14；鹰巢控制三处。战斗栏没有牌，直接进入建造栏。

本次加入 · 建造与后续 · 动荡扣分 · 晚间鸟巢得分 · 得分步骤结束时总分
鸟牌 · F新建鸟巢；Builder与政令保留 · 0 · 三巢得2 · 12
狐狸牌 · 无法建造；清除普通政令牌，换领袖 · 2 · 两巢得1 · 9
狐狸路径扣2分来自两张宰相鸟牌，狐狸牌本身不增加扣分。假定 Despot 尚可选择，换为它，并将两宰相改放移动、建造栏；旧招募狐狸、移动兔子、本次建造狐狸三张普通牌弃掉。此前招募和移动不撤销，晚间仍然计分。本段在晚间得分步骤后结束，抽牌尚未进行。鸟巢分值可核对Learning to Play 第12页的轨道。
鸟牌这一次多保住3分，也保留了更长的政令。但它没有“用完”：以后仍须完成建造，且若后来动荡，留在政令中的这张鸟牌也会计入扣分。两条路径的手牌也不同，分别留下狐狸与鸟，不能只比较当前分数。
设计上的问题因此从“多一个行动有什么好处”变成“新增行动何时变成必须兑现的承诺”。观察对手时，也不能把政令栏当普通行动菜单：对手也许必须移动或建造，不能像猫族一样随时停手。不过本例没有继续模拟对手如何阻断下一轮，因此不宣称这张鸟牌长期一定更优。
角度三：打掉士兵，是否等于清除了影响力？
第三个片段从一场战斗开始，之前的移动已经结束。狐狸空地内有3猫兵、1联盟士兵和1同情标记，没有建筑。猫族有8分，手中一张狐狸牌、一张鸟牌；联盟支持者堆有2张，地图上没有基地。双方不使用伏击或其他战斗效果，猫族不使用野战医院。固定骰子为3和1。
比较正式规则与本站假设改法：只取消联盟的 Guerrilla War 防守换骰能力，其余全部相同。骰子造成的命中仍受本方士兵数限制；承受命中时先移除士兵，再移除建筑或标记。Law 第4.3节，第4页；第8.2.2、8.2.6节，第7页
结算 · 正式规则 · 仅取消防守换骰的假设
猫族命中 · 低骰1，造成1命中 · 高骰3，造成3命中
联盟命中 · 高骰3，但1兵上限，造成1命中 · 低骰1，造成1命中
战后猫兵／联盟兵 · 2／0 · 2／0
同情标记 · 留下 · 移除；多余1命中无目标
猫族分数 · 8 · 9
猫族手牌数／联盟支持者数 · 2／2 · 1／3
假设路径移除了同情标记，触发 Outrage：猫族把狐狸牌交给联盟支持者堆，留下鸟牌。两边都只损失一名士兵，却留下不同的地图影响力和卡牌资源。正式路径没有移除同情，也没有在本片段内移动进去，因此这里不触发 Outrage。两条路径均在战斗及其触发效果处理完毕后结束。
防守换骰在这个例子里主要保护了士兵后面的标记，并没有让仅有一兵的联盟打出3命中。下一次战斗开始时，正式路径的联盟已经没有士兵，条件又会不同。因此，“防守强”需要说明保护什么、持续到何时；只统计伤亡会漏掉设计效果。
出版社的《Hard Cuts》开发日志记录过一次联盟重构：移除旧的 conspiracies 系统后，通过演摆猫族与鹰巢的冲突，逐渐把反抗的后果落实为地图上的同情和基地标记。它启发的本站问题是：题材中的关系，应在哪个可观察的状态上发生变化？这份2018年记录描述开发旧稿，不能代替上表采用的2025年规则，也不能证明取消防守能力就会让游戏更好。
带答案的自查
第一组B为什么由鹰巢控制？猫族1兵加1建筑与鹰巢2兵相等，鹰巢获得平手控制优势；木材不算控制力。
打通木材通路是否必须先消灭B的敌兵？本例不必。移入一兵，取得严格优势即可。
第二组动荡是否撤销招募和移动？不撤销。D3兵、E2兵、F1兵仍在；发生的是政令清除、换领袖与白昼结束。
狐狸路径为什么最终是9分而不是8分？10减去两宰相的2分，再加两鸟巢的晚间1分。
第三组联盟拿到高骰3，为什么只打1命中？它只有一名士兵；换骰没有取消骰子命中的兵力上限。
假设改法为什么还要给联盟一张牌？只取消了防守换骰，移除同情触发的 Outrage 仍然存在。

Root: Why Does One Map Create Three Different Pressures?

The Marquise has wood but cannot spend it on a building. The Eyrie has warriors but may collapse because it cannot fulfil one card. The Alliance can lose its soldiers while leaving influence behind. To understand Root’s asymmetric design, look at where resources are, when actions become compulsory, and what a conflict leaves in place.

This article uses the base factions in the October 13, 2025 Law of Root. The publisher’s product page credits Cole Wehrle with the design. These are three separate snapshots in a four-player base-game setting; the Vagabond does not participate in these passages. No expansions, dominance victories or additional card effects apply. Letters temporarily name clearings. We specify the connections and state needed here, without reconstructing earlier play or presenting a new map or optimal strategy.
Angle one: Enough wood does not mean you can pay

It is the Marquise’s Daylight, with two actions available. She has 8 points and three sawmills on the map. The next sawmill costs 3 wood and scores 3 points; see the track in Learning to Play, page 11. Clearing C, the proposed building site, has an open building slot.

Paths connect A—B—C, with no direct A–C connection. Other routes provide no alternative chain of clearings ruled by the Marquise. The only 3 wood on the entire map are at A. These three clearings contain no pieces beyond those listed, and no sympathy.
Clearing · Marquise warriors / buildings · Eyrie warriors / buildings · Wood · Current ruler
A · 1 / 1 sawmill · 0 / 0 · 3 · Marquise
B · 1 / 1 workshop · 2 / 0 · 0 · Eyrie
C · 3 / 0 · 0 / 0 · 0 · Marquise

B is not ruled by the Marquise: warriors plus buildings give a 2–2 tie, which the Eyrie wins. A’s wood cannot cross B to pay for construction at C. Wood itself does not count toward rule. See Law 2.5, 6.5.4 and 7.2.2, pages 3 and 6.

Compare two choices. Path A stops without building and leaves the state unchanged. Path B spends one March action moving one cat from C to B. March allows up to two moves; only one is taken here. The move is legal because the Marquise rules its origin, C. B now holds two cats plus a workshop against two Eyrie warriors; C still has two cats. The Marquise now rules the entire A–B–C chain.
With the second action, she builds a sawmill at C, removes A’s 3 wood to pay and scores 3 points. The passage ends after that build resolves:
Result · Wood at A · Cats at B / C · New building at C · Marquise points · Actions used here
A: stop · 3 · 1 / 3 · None · 8 · 0
B: move, then build · 0 · 2 / 2 · 1 sawmill · 11 · 2

No enemy was removed and no extra wood was produced. Resource access changed: reallocating one warrior turned existing stock into spendable stock. An interface showing only “3 total wood” would conceal the decision’s central condition.

In your own area game, distinguish total stock, usable stock and the actions needed to open access. Making wood a shared reserve available everywhere would remove this transport condition and change the importance of holding B. That changes more than a handling step. This example establishes immediate results; it does not prove another sawmill is always worth more than the troops, actions and wood retained by stopping.
Angle two: A wild card buys flexibility and creates a future obligation

Move to the Eyrie’s Birdsong. Its leader is the Builder. The existing Decree is below; both Loyal Viziers count as bird cards. The hand contains exactly one fox card and one bird card, neither an ambush nor a dominance card. Compare adding just one of them to Build and retaining the other.
Decree column · Existing cards
Recruit · Bird Loyal Vizier, fox card
Move · Bird Loyal Vizier, rabbit card
Battle · Empty
Build · Empty; add fox or bird now

The Eyrie has only two roosts on the map. Fox clearing D contains two Eyrie warriors and a roost. Adjacent rabbit clearing E also contains two Eyrie warriors and a roost. E connects to mouse clearing F, which is empty and has an open slot. The Eyrie has 16 warriors in supply and 10 points. There are no enemies, ruins or other effects in these three clearings. No other fox clearing is ruled by the Eyrie, and the omitted map supplies no extra action targets.

Neither path crafts cards. Both resolve the first two columns identically: recruit twice at D, increasing its warriors from two to four; use the bird move to move one from D to E, then the rabbit move to move one from E to F. D now has three, E two and F one, with fourteen in supply. The Eyrie rules all three. Battle is empty, so proceed to Build.

The bird path can put a third roost at F. The fox path cannot build at mouse clearing F, while D, the only ruled fox clearing, already has a roost. The action cannot be fulfilled, causing immediate turmoil. See Law 7.4–7.8, pages 6–7.
Card added · Build and aftermath · Turmoil loss · Evening roost points · Total after the scoring step
Bird · Build at F; retain Builder and Decree · 0 · Three roosts score 2 · 12
Fox · Cannot build; purge ordinary Decree cards and change leader · 2 · Two roosts score 1 · 9

The fox path loses 2 points for the two bird Viziers; the fox card adds no penalty. Assume the Despot is available: select it and reassign the Viziers to Move and Build. Discard the ordinary Recruit fox, Move rabbit and newly added Build fox. Earlier recruits and moves remain; Evening scoring still happens. This passage stops after that scoring step, before drawing cards. Track values are visible in Learning to Play, page 12.

The bird preserves three more points now and keeps a longer Decree. But it is not spent after use: another build remains compulsory on future turns, and this bird would add to the penalty in a later turmoil. The retained hand card also differs—fox in one path, bird in the other—so present points are not the whole comparison.

The design question changes from “What does one more action provide?” to “When does an added action become a promise that must be fulfilled?” An opponent’s Decree is not an ordinary action menu. The Eyrie may have to move or build when the Marquise could simply stop. We have not simulated how opponents might block the next turn, so this is not a claim that the bird is always the better long-term choice.
Angle three: Removing soldiers need not remove influence

The third passage begins with a battle; any earlier movement has already ended. A fox clearing contains three cats, one Alliance warrior and one sympathy token, with no buildings. The Marquise has 8 points and two hand cards, one fox and one bird. The Alliance has two supporters and no bases anywhere on the map. Neither side uses an ambush or another battle effect; the Marquise declines Field Hospitals. Fix the dice at 3 and 1.

Compare the official rule with a site-created hypothetical change: remove only the Alliance’s Guerrilla War reversal of defensive dice. Everything else stays fixed. Rolled hits still cannot exceed that side’s warrior count, and warriors are removed before buildings or tokens. See Law 4.3, page 4, and 8.2.2 and 8.2.6, page 7.
Resolution · Official rule · Hypothetical removal of defensive reversal only
Marquise hits · Low die 1: one hit · High die 3: three hits
Alliance hits · High die 3, capped by one warrior: one hit · Low die 1: one hit
Cats / Alliance warriors afterward · 2 / 0 · 2 / 0
Sympathy · Remains · Removed; one excess hit has no target
Marquise points · 8 · 9
Marquise hand size / Alliance supporters · 2 / 2 · 1 / 3

Removing sympathy in the hypothetical path triggers Outrage. The Marquise gives the fox card to the supporters stack and retains the bird. Both paths lose exactly one warrior per side, but leave different influence on the map and different card resources. The official path removes no sympathy and includes no movement into the clearing during this passage, so neither triggers Outrage here. Each path ends after the battle and its triggered effects resolve.

In this example, defensive reversal mainly protects the token behind the warrior. It does not let a lone Alliance warrior inflict three hits. If another battle begins, the official path now has no Alliance warriors there, so the conditions change again. “Strong defence” needs an object and a time horizon: what survives, and for how long? Casualty counts alone miss this effect.

The publisher’s Hard Cuts development diary records an Alliance redesign: after removing the old conspiracies system, staging a Marquise–Eyrie conflict helped express rebellion through sympathy and base pieces on the map. Our resulting design question is: where should a thematic relationship produce an observable change of state? This 2018 account describes a development draft. It does not replace the 2025 rules used above or establish that removing defensive reversal improves the game.
Self-checks with answers
Why does the Eyrie rule B in the first example? One cat plus one building ties two Eyrie warriors, and the Eyrie wins ties for rule. Wood adds nothing to that count.
Must the Marquise destroy the enemy at B to open access to wood? Not here. Adding a warrior establishes a strict majority without a battle.
Does turmoil undo the second example’s recruits and moves? No. D retains three warriors, E two and F one. The purge, leader change and end of Daylight do not rewind them.
Why does the fox path end on 9 rather than 8 points? Start at 10, lose two for the Viziers, then score one for two roosts in Evening.
Why does the Alliance’s high die of 3 cause only one hit in the third example? It has one warrior. Reversing the dice does not remove the warrior cap on rolled hits.
Why give the Alliance a card under the hypothetical change? Only defensive dice reversal was removed. Outrage for removing sympathy still applies.

Radlands：同样一点水，为什么早一回合就不同？
《Radlands》让两人用水打出人物、安排事件、发动能力，以摧毁对方三座营地为目标。人物可以挡在营地前；有些威胁却沿着公开的事件队列逼近。理解它的关键，不只是数资源，还要看资源何时能花、伤害落到谁身上，以及对手还能回应几次。
本文采用官方英文规则 V2.1 的基本游戏部分，仅用原有34张营地，不加入 Cult of Chrome。当前 Roxley 产品页展示的是包含扩展的 Complete 包装；页面下载入口标着2024.11.13，实际文件第3页写 V2.1、封底标©2026，不能混为同一个日期。
下文三组都是本站原创局部对照，不是完整对局历史或最优打法。每组两人都已失去两座营地，仅剩下文指明的一座；这使结局容易追踪。未列出的人物、手牌和队列均为空，水塔与 Raiders 未被指定时都在各自桌面待取区；牌库足够，无须重洗，弃牌堆中的牌不参与本段。指定抽牌供复算，不表示玩家预知牌顶。其余能力不用，也没有改变本段费用、时序的特性。
角度一：保存的不是水片，而是下一回合的一次兑换
A只剩完好的 Garage，B只剩完好的 Supply Depot。现在是A行动阶段末，A余1水，手中仅有 Bombardment，水塔（Water Silo）仍在桌面。Bombardment需要4水，事件时间为3；两边队列都空。我们比较A买下水塔留手，与直接结束。牌面及水塔规则，第7、11页
接下来固定同一段回应：B在自己的补充阶段抽到 Cult Leader、拿3水，选择不行动，归还全部水；A下一回合先处理空队列，再抽到 Gunner、拿3水。普通余水不能跨回合保留；先手首回合只有1水的例外已过去。回合顺序，第9页
路径 · A上回合最后1水 · A下回合支付前 · 能否按指定路线打出4水事件
保存 · 支付1，把水塔拿入手 · 3水，弃用水塔再得1，共4 · 能；付4，把 Bombardment 放在3格
不保存 · 结束时归还 · 只有3水 · 不能；保留 Bombardment，结束并归还3水
保存路径结束时A只剩 Gunner 一张手牌，水为0；水塔回桌面，Bombardment 留在队列，尚未生效。不保存路径A有两张手牌，队列仍空。双方最后一座营地都未受伤，游戏继续。这里没有把其他抽牌、弃牌或能力产水的路线算进来。
保存路径没有制造免费的额外收入：前一回合付了1，后一回合才兑换1。它改变的是支出集中在哪一回合，使3水补给能够跨过4水门槛。如果现在才买水塔再立即弃用，水量只是3−1＋1＝3，无法补上差额。可重复拿取，不等于可重复增值。
给原创游戏设计储存机制时，可以先写出一个超过常规补给的费用，再比较储存前后能否支付。还要分别问：储存有没有占用当前机会，是否消耗卡牌，兑换后是否返还容器。水塔保存在手牌里，回桌后还能再买；这些状态变化比一句“余量可以保存”更具体。
角度二：前排保护了谁，也决定谁失去能力
换一个快照：A只剩完好的 Railgun；B只剩完好的 Supply Depot，营地前有一个健康的 Repair Bot，已经在此前回合入场。B正处于行动阶段末，水为0，手中仅有 Magnus Karv。B弃用这张牌，依其弃牌图标从牌库顶取得一个背面朝上的 punk；不用支付该人物的打出费用。Punk没有能力，受一次伤害即被摧毁，背面朝上放回牌库顶，不能偷看。图标和人物规则，第6、8、10页
这列原来只有一个人物，所以新punk既可放在机器人前，也可放在后；两种摆法都达到每列两人的上限。B结束。A随后处理空队列，抽到 Gunner、取得3水，再支付2水使用已就绪的 Railgun，对该列最前方人物造成一次普通伤害。Railgun牌面第5页；保护与伤害第7–8页；就绪第11页
从对手方向看，由前至后 · 这次伤害如何结算 · A结束时B的局面
Punk→Repair Bot→营地 · Punk被摧毁并回牌库顶 · 剩1个人物：健康机器人；营地仍受保护
Repair Bot→Punk→营地 · 机器人转横受伤，留在原位 · 剩2个人物：受伤机器人和punk；营地仍受保护
两条路径A都归还余下1水、留下 Gunner；B手牌为空，Magnus Karv在弃牌堆。第二条路径的punk仍在场。两边营地均未被摧毁，游戏继续。
数人数，第二条路径似乎更好；看可用能力，第一条保住了健康机器人。受伤人物不能发动能力，而受伤营地仍可能就绪。Repair Bot的主动恢复能力收费2水，它能否在之后帮忙还取决于是否存在合法受损目标，不能把“健康”直接当成已经获得一次治疗。
保护也没有因为人物受伤就自动消失：第二条路径中，受伤机器人仍在最前面，继续挡住后方。下一次普通伤害的目标因此不同。两种摆法用同样一张弃牌制造同样一个punk，却把后续损失分配给不同对象。做站位原型时，应同时记录位置、受伤状态与可用动作；只比较场上数量，会漏掉行动能力的变化。
角度三：提前结算，拿走的是对手的一次修复机会
第三组中，A只剩健康的 Garage，B只剩受伤的 Supply Depot，前面有一个punk。B手中仅有 Repair Bot。A刚结束补充阶段，手中仅有 Magnus Karv、有3水，Garage尚未使用。A的 Raiders 本回合事件阶段从2格移到1格，队列没有其他事件。
到达1格不会在同一个事件阶段再结算：事件阶段先结算原本在1格的事件，再移动剩余事件。Garage的能力收费1水，产生一次 raid；Raiders已在1格时，这次raid会立即使它结算。它让对手选择一座自己的营地受伤，能够越过人物保护。Garage牌面第5页；Raid与事件顺序第9页
路径 · 按顺序发生的事 · 结果
A现在花1水 · Garage触发raid；B只能选择最后的受伤营地；再次受伤，摧毁 · A立即获胜，尚余2水；无需等回合结束
A等待自然倒计时 · A归还3水结束；B抽 Gunner、拿3水；花1打出 Repair Bot，放在punk之后；入场特性恢复营地，B归还余下2水 · A下一回合Raiders结算，只把健康营地打成受伤，尚未获胜
延后路径中的机器人刚入场，不能马上使用收费2水的主动能力；这里生效的是它的入场恢复特性。该列只有punk，后排仍有空间，恢复目标是营地而非机器人自己。Repair Bot牌面第6页；入场、恢复及就绪第8、10–11页
继续把延后路径收完：Raiders回到A桌面待取区；A补充抽到 Looter、拿3水，然后选择结束，归还3水，留下 Magnus Karv 与 Looter 两张手牌。B还握着 Gunner，机器人与punk都存活，最后营地仍受伤。立即路径则已经终止，不能给B补演一回合来“挽救”。
提前那一步没有增加伤害次数，两条路线都只结算一次Raiders。差别是受击前有没有出现一次恢复。公开倒计时因此不只是等待标记，它把回应窗口摆在桌面上；支付1水，可以改变窗口是否存在。但本例固定B确实有机器人并选择修复，不证明所有事件都应加速，也不证明对手总能修好。

Radlands: Why Does One Water Matter More a Turn Earlier?

In Radlands, two players spend water to play people, schedule events, and use abilities, aiming to destroy the opponent's three camps. People can stand in front of camps, while some threats approach along a public event queue. Understanding the game involves more than counting resources: when can they be spent, who receives damage, and how many responses remain available?

This article uses the base-game portion of the official English V2.1 rules and only the original 34 camps, excluding Cult of Chrome. The current Roxley product page presents Complete packaging that includes the expansion. Its download entry is dated November 13, 2024, but the actual file identifies V2.1 on page 3 and ©2026 on its back cover. These are different dates for different things.

The three comparisons below are our original local constructions, not complete game histories or optimal strategies. In each, both players have already lost two camps and retain only the camp specified below, making the ending easier to follow. Unlisted people, hands, and queues are empty. Unless specified otherwise, each player's Water Silo and Raiders are in their respective table areas, outside the hand and event queue. The deck has enough cards without reshuffling, and cards in the discard pile do not participate. Specified draws make the examples reproducible; players do not know the deck's order. Other abilities remain unused, and no traits modify these costs or timing.
Angle one: Store a future exchange, not an unspent water disc

A retains an undamaged Garage; B retains an undamaged Supply Depot. Near the end of A's Actions phase, A has one water left and only Bombardment in hand, with Water Silo still on the table. Bombardment costs four water and has event time 3; both queues are empty. Compare buying and retaining Water Silo with ending immediately. Card image and Water Silo rules, pp.7, 11

Fix the same response in both branches. During B's Replenish phase, B draws Cult Leader and takes three water, then chooses no actions and returns all water. On A's next turn, A handles the empty event queue, draws Gunner, and takes three water. Ordinary water cannot carry over; the starting player's one-water first-turn exception is already past. Turn sequence, p.9
Branch · A's last water on the previous turn · Available before payment next turn · Can A play the four-water event by this route?
Store · Pay one to take Water Silo into hand · Three water, plus one from junking Water Silo, totaling four · Yes: pay four and place Bombardment in space 3
Do not store · Return it at turn end · Three water · No: retain Bombardment, end, and return three water

The stored branch ends with only Gunner in A's hand and zero water. Water Silo is back on the table; Bombardment remains queued and has not resolved. The other branch leaves A with two cards and an empty queue. Both remaining camps are undamaged, so play continues. This comparison does not include additional draws, junk effects, or other abilities that could provide water.

Storing has not created free income: A paid one on the earlier turn and exchanged it for one later. It changes which turn can concentrate the spending, allowing a three-water replenishment to cross a four-water threshold. Buying and immediately junking Water Silo now would produce only 3−1+1=3 water, leaving the shortfall unchanged. Repeated access does not imply repeated profit.

When designing storage for an original game, write down a cost above the normal replenishment amount, then compare whether it becomes payable with storage. Separately ask whether storage consumes a current opportunity, whether it consumes a card, and whether the container returns after redemption. Water Silo stays in hand and can be bought again after returning to the table. Those state changes are more precise than simply saying that surplus can be saved.
Angle two: Front positions decide who stays protected and who loses an ability

Use a new snapshot. A retains an undamaged Railgun. B retains an undamaged Supply Depot with a healthy Repair Bot in front, played on an earlier turn. Near the end of B's Actions phase, B has zero water and only Magnus Karv in hand. B junks that card, using its junk icon to take a facedown punk from the deck's top, without paying Magnus Karv's play cost. A punk has no abilities. One damage destroys it and returns it facedown to the top of the deck without anyone looking at its face. Icons and people, pp.6, 8, 10

The column previously contained one person, so the new punk can go either in front of or behind Repair Bot. Either arrangement reaches the limit of two people per column. B ends. A then handles an empty queue, draws Gunner, takes three water, and pays two to use the ready Railgun, dealing one ordinary damage to the front person in this column. Railgun image, p.5; protection and damage, pp.7–8; readiness, p.11
Front to back, viewed from the opponent · Damage resolution · B's position when A ends
Punk→Repair Bot→camp · Destroy the punk and return it to the deck's top · One person remains: a healthy Repair Bot; the camp is still protected
Repair Bot→punk→camp · Turn Repair Bot sideways as damaged; leave it in place · Two people remain: damaged Repair Bot and the punk; the camp is still protected

In both branches A returns the remaining one water and keeps Gunner. B has no hand, and Magnus Karv is in the discard pile. The second branch's punk remains in play. Neither remaining camp has been destroyed, so play continues.

Counting people makes the second branch look stronger; counting usable abilities shows what the first branch preserved. A damaged person cannot use abilities, whereas a damaged camp can still be ready. Repair Bot's activated restore ability costs two water. Whether it can help later also depends on having a legal damaged target: being healthy does not itself deliver a heal.

Protection does not automatically vanish when a person takes damage. In the second branch the damaged bot still stands at the front and shields the cards behind it, changing the target of the next ordinary hit. The two placements create the same punk from the same discarded card but assign future losses to different objects. In a positioning prototype, record position, damage, and available actions together. Counting objects alone misses changes in what those objects can do.
Angle three: Resolving earlier removes a chance to repair

In the third comparison, A retains a healthy Garage. B retains a damaged Supply Depot with a punk in front, and has only Repair Bot in hand. A has just completed Replenish, holds only Magnus Karv, has three water, and has not used Garage. During this turn's Events phase, A's Raiders advanced from space 2 to space 1. No other events are queued.

Arriving in space 1 does not resolve an event again during that Events phase. The phase first resolves the event already in space 1, then moves the others. Garage costs one water to produce a raid effect. If Raiders is already in space 1, that raid resolves it immediately. Raiders makes the opponent choose one of their camps to damage, bypassing people protecting it. Garage image, p.5; Raid and event order, p.9
Branch · Sequence · Result
A spends one now · Garage triggers a raid; B must choose the last damaged camp; another damage destroys it · A wins immediately with two water unspent, without waiting for turn end

A waits for the normal countdown · A ends and returns three water; B draws Gunner and takes three water; B pays one to play Repair Bot behind the punk, restores the camp with its entry trait, and returns the remaining two water · On A's next turn, Raiders only changes the healthy camp to damaged; A has not won

The delayed branch's Repair Bot has just entered play and cannot immediately use its two-water activated ability. The effect used here is its entry trait. The column has only a punk, leaving space behind it; the restore target is the camp, not Repair Bot itself. Repair Bot image, p.6; entering play, restore, and readiness, pp.8, 10–11

Finish the delayed branch: Raiders returns to A's table area. A replenishes by drawing Looter and taking three water, then chooses to end, returning all three and retaining Magnus Karv and Looter. B retains Gunner; Repair Bot and the punk survive, and the last camp remains damaged. The immediate branch has already ended, so B cannot receive an extra turn to rescue it.

Acceleration did not add a hit: each route resolved Raiders exactly once. What changed was whether a restore happened before the hit. The public countdown therefore exposes a response window, and spending one water can change whether that window exists. This example fixes both B's possession of Repair Bot and the decision to restore. It does not show that every event should be accelerated or that opponents can always repair their camps.
Self-checks with answers
Can buying and immediately junking Water Silo turn three water into four? No. Paying one and gaining one leaves three.
Does the damaged Repair Bot still protect cards behind it in angle two? Yes. It remains at the front, although its person ability is unavailable.
Does a punk hit by Railgun go to the discard pile? No. Return it facedown to the deck's top without looking at its face.
Does Raiders resolve in the same Events phase when moving from space 2 to space 1? No. That phase's space-1 resolution happened before movement.
Why can the newly played Repair Bot restore the camp in angle three? Its entry trait does so; its two-water activated ability was not used.

Spirit Island：没有消灭敌人，为什么局面已经变好了？
把侵略者推到隔壁、让达汉活过一次攻击、让最后一座城镇消失，表面上都是改动几个棋子。在《Spirit Island》中，这些动作还会改变敌人的生产机会、反击来源，甚至整局的胜利条件。设计者需要沿着结算继续看，而不是只数这次拿掉几个敌人。
本文采用出版社产品页所链接的英文基础规则：32页，第28页版权栏为2016—2018，文件未明确印次。排除扩展、对手、剧本与主题地图，不使用枯萎卡；另应用官方FAQ的初始枯萎勘误：供应池按5×玩家数＋1设置，因此单人6枚、双人11枚。这不是每人额外加一枚；岛上初始枯萎从盒中另取。
以下三个独立局面是本站原创的局部状态，不是从开局逐轮重建的对局或真人试玩。各神灵已合法完成成长、取得相应牌，并有足够出牌额度；没有未列出的能力介入。未列土地照常结算，且不使游戏提前结束或改变所列土地。每例明确检查到哪里，不把一次局部成功当作整局获胜。
角度一：推走一个探索者，也可能少造一座城镇
双人局使用 River Surges in Sunlight（下称河灵）与 Lightning’s Swift Strike（雷灵）。相邻的丛林J和山地M都没有枯萎、达汉或建筑；J只有一个探索者与河灵的一枚存在，M没有侵略者。河灵另有存在，雷灵也仍在岛上。当前肆虐湿地、建造丛林，本轮随后探索沙地；这些行动不在M发生。全岛另有城市，因此局部清空J不会触发当前惊惧I的胜利。
两位神灵各有1能量，只打下述一张牌，各付1后都余0。河灵的 Wash Away 是慢能力，范围1，可以推走目标地至多三个探索者／城镇；J有自己的存在，距离0符合范围。雷灵的 Lightning’s Boon 是快能力，目标为任意神灵，本次指定河灵，让它本轮至多两个慢能力可以按快能力使用。本例不使用两位神灵的先天能力。Wash Away原卡图；Lightning’s Boon原卡图
比较河灵接受加速与仍保持慢速，两边都已经支付上述费用：
时点 · 作为快能力使用 · 仍作为慢能力使用
快能力阶段 · 雷灵先结算支援；河灵把J的探索者推到相邻M。 · 雷灵支援照常结算，河灵不选加速，暂不移动。
侵略者建造 · J没有侵略者，不建造；M不是丛林，不建造。 · J有探索者且城镇、城市均为0，增加一座城镇。
本轮慢能力阶段结束 · J空，M有一个探索者。已用过的Wash Away不能再用。 · 河灵把J的探索者及新城镇一起推到M，数量2没有超过上限3；J空。
探索沙地不向J、M加棋子；其他土地的探索结果不影响这份两地账本。两条路线都不产生恐惧，没有任何棋子被摧毁。可是慢速分支比快速分支多了一座城镇：它仍在M，下一次被影响时要照常处理。推走不是从游戏里抹掉。建造及阶段顺序见规则第8—10页，推走与单次使用见第17、19页
设计启发是把“打断下一步生产”也计入动作的价值。本例加速没有增加移动数量，却赶在建造条件检查之前清空了J。但它不能证明快能力总更强：雷灵花了1能量与一次出牌，M也接收了威胁。若只看J最后都是空地，会漏掉成本和邻地存量；若对手规则允许空地建造，这个推论也未必成立。
角度二：达汉不是替土地挡伤害的护盾
另开一个单人河灵局。某湿地W正要肆虐，里面有一个探索者、一座城镇、一座城市、两个完好的达汉与河灵的一枚存在；没有枯萎。河灵在别处还有存在，全岛别处还有城市。枯萎供应池现余4枚，恐惧池四枚都尚未移出，本轮没有待结算恐惧牌。
河灵此前合法获得了次级能力 Sap the Strength of Multitudes。本轮只打这张牌，付0能量、占一次出牌，在快阶段选W。它的基础效果是防御5，范围0，W有河灵存在，所以不用满足增加范围的风元素条件。规则第16页原卡与目标图示，第18页防御说明
侵略者的总伤害是1＋2＋3＝6。防御使它降至1；土地承受1，达汉整体也承受1，不是先让达汉接伤、再把剩余伤害交给土地。土地未达到2，不加枯萎；一个达汉受1伤但未死亡，两个达汉都能反击，共造成4伤害。
本例把其中3伤害给城市、1伤害给探索者，恰好摧毁二者；城镇仍然完好。城市被摧毁产生2恐惧，探索者不产生恐惧：四枚恐惧标记中两枚移到已产生区域，尚未获得恐惧牌。枯萎池仍有4枚，河灵存在保留，两个达汉存活。伤害、反击与生命值见规则第9、15—16页
从同一状态改为放弃这张牌的效果，则6伤害同时打向土地与达汉。土地增加一枚枯萎，供应池4→3，并摧毁W中河灵的一枚存在；原来无枯萎，所以不连锁。两个达汉各需2伤害即死亡，不能把6伤害分散成“都受一点”；没有幸存者反击，三种侵略者全部留下，也不产生恐惧。河灵别处仍有存在，所以此时并未因存在归零而输掉。
本轮后续建造丛林、探索沙地，均不再改变W；没有其他能力影响它。时间流逝时，成功防御分支中受伤的达汉恢复，防御效果结束。这里防御既减少损失，又保留了反击的来源。但防御牌本身没有造成那4点伤害；若W没有达汉，同样防御5只能挡伤，不能自动清除侵略者。也不能把“伤害被防到0”误当成“跳过肆虐”：前者仍可让达汉反击，后者没有这次反击。
角度三：恐惧不仅给奖励，还会改变终点
第三个单人河灵局从快能力阶段开始。全岛侵略者恰有一座完好城镇和三个探索者，没有城市；城镇在沿海地C，河灵在C有存在，另处也有存在。惊惧等级仍为I。基础恐惧牌采用3／3／3分组，已经获得并结算最前面的两张；再获得一张就露出惊惧II分隔板。四枚恐惧标记中已有3枚在已产生区域，池中只剩1枚。枯萎池尚有4枚，侵略者牌堆未空，无其他结束条件触发。
河灵在神灵阶段有2能量，只打 Flash Floods 并付2，余0。它是快能力，范围1；C中的存在使目标合法。沿海地满足额外伤害条件，合计1＋1＝2，全部打给城镇，恰好摧毁。Flash Floods原卡图
接着产生摧毁城镇的1恐惧：进度3／4→4／4，最上方恐惧牌移入待结算区，四枚标记回到恐惧池。新露出的惊惧II立即生效。此时全岛既无城镇也无城市，满足新的胜利条件；三个探索者仍在岛上也可以获胜，不必等下一次恐惧阶段翻开刚获得的牌。规则第6页恐惧牌组装，第12页胜利与等级图示
只把初始恐惧进度改成2／4，其他条件和动作相同：城镇照样被摧毁，但恐惧只到3／4，尚未拿到下一张牌，惊惧仍为I。三个探索者使“全岛没有侵略者”的条件不成立，所以这次能力结束时尚未获胜；这不等于已经失败，游戏仍继续。
两边移除了同一个棋子，区别来自全局恐惧进度与将要露出的分隔板。若原型只把恐惧写成“攒满获得奖励”，就会漏掉它还在改变需要清除哪些敌人。也不能把“所有城镇消失”写成恒定胜利条件：它需要对应等级，且全岛不能还有城市。
作者亲述与本站分析
R. Eric Reuss 在规则第29页的署名设计笔记中说，创意来自一次殖民主题游戏中的疑问：既有居民的视角为何被抽掉？他希望用抵抗殖民的立场构造游戏，并选择了虚构冲突，而非模拟某一场具体历史战争。原文“Design Notes”
这是作者的创作回忆。本站的分析是：改变观察立场后，还要让规则决定什么值得保护、什么算赶走威胁。上面的土地、达汉与恐惧分别承担这些工作；三个算例并不能证明游戏消除了合作游戏中的主导玩家问题，也不是对真实殖民历史的验证。
带答案的自查
角度一两边最后J都空了，为什么结果不同？慢速分支已经在建造时增加一座城镇，它被推到M而没有消失。
接受加速后，Wash Away能在慢阶段再用一次吗？不能；加速改变时点，没有额外使用次数。
角度二防御后的1伤害，是被达汉吸收后土地免伤吗？不是；土地与达汉分别承受1，土地因为低于2才不加枯萎。
为什么受伤达汉仍能造成2反击伤害？它没有达到2生命值的死亡门槛；每个幸存达汉反击2，与剩余生命值不是同一数值。
角度三还剩三个探索者，为何能够结束？刚升到惊惧II，胜利检查只要求没有城镇、城市；若仍在I就不行。
